user: Do I need an IBM Cloud account to start using the Analytics Engine for V 3 C L I?
assistant: Yes, you need an IBM Cloud account to start using the Analytics Engine. See Getting started with IBM Analytics Engine to learn more about the service and to start using it. You will also find tutorials and code samples to get you off to a fast start.
[The End of Previous Conversation]

[The Start of Current Turn Question]
What about pricing? Is there a free trial period to start?
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
Yes, IBM Cloud offers a 30-day free trial for new users. Go to the IBM Cloud console and create an account. You're asked to enter your credit card information to secure your account and verify your identity. There are no costs that are associated with signing up, and you can try out IBM Cloud for free. You pay only for billable services that you choose to use, with no long-term contracts or commitments. You're set up with a Pay-As-You-Go account, and you can access the full IBM Cloud catalog, including all Lite and Free plans. You receive a $200 credit to help get you started. You can use the $200 credit on IBM Cloud products that are used in the first 30 days. During this period, you can explore and use various services, including IBM Analytics Engine, free of charge up to certain usage limits. For more information, you can visit the IBM Cloud website or contact IBM sales representatives.
[The End of Reference Answer]

[The Start of Assistant's Answer]
Page 1 says IBM Cloud trial accounts provide time-limited access to selected service plans, including Lite and Free plans, without financial commitment. To qualify, validate your institution credentials through “Harness the Power of IBM” or contact your educational program or course leader.

However, the provided information does not specify Analytics Engine pricing, whether Analytics Engine is included in the trial, or how long the trial lasts. The pricing details shown on page 1 apply to Direct Link, not Analytics Engine.
[The End of Assistant's Answer]

[The Start of Document]
Trial account 

Trial accounts offer timed access to a limited range of service plans and allow you to test out the platform without financial commitment. You can access Lite service plans and Free plans for a limited time with a trial account. To qualify for a trial account, go to [Harness the Power of IBM](https://ibm.biz/academic) and validate your institution credentials or reach out to your educational program or course leader. If you don't have an account, select 'Register with a Code' during IBM Cloud registration to apply a code. If you have an account, go to the [Account settings](https://cloud.ibm.com/account/settings) page in the console to apply the code.

In terms of cost, what do I pay for? 

There are two pricing plans: metered and unmetered. Metered has a port fee and bill per GB egressed across the Direct Link. Unmetered billing has a higher port fee and no usage charges, which are ideal for customers who consistently egress traffic across their direct link.
* Can I change billing options after my direct link is provisioned?

 Can I change billing options after my direct link is provisioned? 

Yes, you can change billing options after a direct link is provisioned, regardless of whether you chose global or local routing. For example, to change from metered to unmetered billing, navigate to the Details page of the direct link and click Edit. In the side panel, select Unmetered in the Billing section, review the updated information, then agree to the prerequisites and click Submit.

It discusses an academic trial-account process from the provided document, but the reference describes IBM Cloud’s standard 30-day free trial for new users, including the $200 credit, the credit-card requirement for verification, and charges only for billable services used. It also incorrectly claims the information does not specify the trial length, when the reference does.

The answer does appropriately avoid applying the Direct Link pricing details to Analytics Engine, but it fails to answer the user’s question about pricing and whether there is a free trial, and it introduces eligibility requirements not present in the reference. Since the document itself does not support the reference’s standard-trial details, the response is consistent with the supplied document but incomplete relative to the reference answer.
